title.t: Tomato Doctor: A Tamil-First Conversational Crop-Disease Diagnosis System on a Probabilistic Knowledge Graph with Information-Gain Questioning and Weather-Aware Advisory

runs.t: Smallholder tomato growers describe crop problems in colloquial, mixed-script language, often without a usable photograph, while most digital diagnosis tools are image classifiers trained on laboratory photographs. We present

, a Tamil-first diagnosis system that reasons over a probabilistic knowledge graph (KG) of 17 diseases and pests, 45 observable symptoms, 247 Tamil, English and Tanglish lay-terms and 30 cited treatments. A concept-level language layer with Tamil stem matching, negation scope and IDF-weighted phrase coverage turns free text into reliability-weighted symptom evidence; a Bayesian engine with an explicit

hypothesis fuses that evidence with a calibrated leaf-photo classifier and a weather-driven prior, and asks the follow-up question with the highest expected information gain. Confirmed outcomes update Beta-distributed KG edge weights, and an advisory layer turns local hourly weather into spray windows, resistance-aware rotation and a dated schedule. On 85 held-out farmer descriptions with simulated noisy dialogues, top-1 accuracy rises from 63.5% (95% CI 52.9–74.1) for the fuzzy-matching prototype to 96.8% (94.5–98.5), while confidently wrong answers fall from 10.6% to 1.2%; information-gain questioning needs 2.1 questions on average, 37% fewer than a weight-variance heuristic at equal accuracy. Under field-like photo degradation the classifier alone drops to 36.4%, whereas fusing the same photo with the dialogue recovers 67.8%. Starting from a deliberately corrupted graph, confirmation-driven learning raises accuracy from 81.2% to 93.6% over 1,500 simulated consultations and nearly halves the mean edge-weight error, whereas the prototype’s update rule increases it. A request costs 3.7 ms on a laptop CPU.
Knowledge graphs, plant disease diagnosis, Bayesian inference, expected information gain, low-resource languages, Tamil, decision support systems, precision agriculture.

Early, correct identification of a crop disease decides whether a farmer sprays the right product at the right time or loses part of a harvest. Deep convolutional networks recognise diseases in curated leaf photographs with high accuracy [1], [2], yet their accuracy falls sharply on images taken in the field, with cluttered backgrounds, multiple symptoms and variable lighting [2], [3]. Moreover, an image-only tool assumes that the farmer can and will produce a clear photograph, and it cannot use the most informative signal the farmer already has: what they saw, said in their own words.
For Tamil-speaking growers that description is colloquial, agglutinative and frequently code-mixed with English or written in Latin script (“Tanglish”), e.g.

(“white dust-like stuff on the leaf”). Such descriptions are also genuinely ambiguous: “white dust” fits both powdery mildew and a whitefly infestation, two problems with entirely different treatments. A useful system must therefore (i) understand informal multilingual text robustly, (ii) recognise when the evidence is insufficient and ask the

question that best separates the remaining candidates, (iii) remain usable when the photograph is poor, (iv) adapt treatment advice to the local weather that determines both disease pressure and whether a spray will wash off, and (v) improve as farmers confirm or correct its answers.

A first prototype of this project stored diseases, symptoms, Tamil lay-terms and treatments in a Neo4j graph, matched farmer text to lay-terms with whole-phrase fuzzy matching and summed edge weights to rank diseases. Analysing it revealed failure modes that motivate this work: shared filler words caused spurious matches, negation was ignored, answers to follow-up questions did not influence the ranking, and a single rejection decayed edge weights for all future users.

runs.t: The PlantVillage collection [4] enabled convolutional models that reach high accuracy on held-out laboratory images [1], [2]. The same studies, and a dedicated analysis of influencing factors [3], report substantial degradation under field conditions caused by background, illumination, symptom variability and co-occurring disorders. We use such a classifier as one source of evidence and quantify how fusion with dialogue changes its behaviour under degradation.

Normative expert systems such as Pathfinder [5] and the probabilistic reformulation of INTERNIST-1/QMR [6] represent diagnosis as Bayesian inference over findings; Pathfinder additionally chooses the next finding to observe by its expected value of information, and the expected information gain of an experiment goes back to Lindley [7]. We adapt this line of work to an agricultural KG whose findings arrive through noisy language understanding rather than structured entry, and model that noise explicitly.
Agricultural knowledge graphs and conversational agents

Knowledge graphs organise entities and typed relations for retrieval and reasoning [8]. AgriKG [9] extracts agricultural entities from web text into a graph for entity retrieval and question answering. FarmChat [10] showed that a speech-based conversational agent built from Kisan Call Centre logs can meet the information needs of low-literate farmers in India. Our system differs in that the KG is
and drives an adaptive diagnostic dialogue, and in that weights change with verified field outcomes.

IndicNLPSuite [11] provides corpora and multilingual models for Indian languages, and large-scale weakly supervised speech recognition [12] and multimodal large language models [13] now transcribe Tamil speech. Colloquial agricultural symptom descriptions remain a low-resource domain, which motivates our lightweight, inspectable concept lexicon and the use of an LLM only as a constrained entity linker.

Disease forecasters convert weather into infection risk: FAST [14] and its TOM-CAST derivative accumulate daily disease-severity values (DSVs) from leaf wetness and temperature for early blight [15]; the Smith Period and the more sensitive Hutton Criteria flag late-blight risk from consecutive warm, humid days [16]. We use these models, together with rules derived from a tomato disease dataset [17], as a prior for diagnosis and as an early warning.

Fig. 1 shows the architecture. A Tamil-first progressive web application collects free text, voice, a leaf photograph, location, and optional tapped symptoms, severity, extent and previously sprayed products. Four extractors turn these inputs into evidence: the concept matcher (Section V), an LLM entity linker for speech, a leaf-photo classifier, and a field-context service that fetches hourly weather and nearby outbreak reports. The reasoning core maintains a posterior over diseases (Section VI); while no hypothesis is confident it asks the most informative question, otherwise it returns a diagnosis with an evidence-level explanation and a weather-aware treatment plan (Section VII). Farmer confirmations and expert curation close the loop (Section VIII).

runs.t: Symptoms, favourable conditions and treatments for nine diseases are drawn from a tomato disease dataset compiled from more than 40 authoritative sources [17]; the remaining entries are standard extension guidance and are labelled as such in the graph and the user interface. Of the 30 treatments, 21 cite the dataset. Tamil lay-terms were written by the authors, including the 28 phrases of the original prototype, and the graph grows at run time through expert curation (Section VIII). A referential-integrity validator checks the graph before every load.

runs.t: For voice input, the recording is converted to 16 kHz mono WAV in the browser and sent to a multimodal LLM (Gemini [13]) with a JSON schema whose symptom and treatment fields are

. The model returns a verbatim transcript, linked symptoms with a confidence and the quoted words, severity, the estimated share of affected plants, duration, crop stage and products already sprayed; it is explicitly instructed not to diagnose. The output is validated (unknown identifiers dropped, numbers clamped), the transcript is also passed through the concept matcher, and LLM-linked symptoms are used only where the matcher found nothing. The LLM thus widens recall without being able to introduce a disease or a dosage that is not in the curated graph. The leaf classifier uses a frozen ImageNet MobileNetV3-Large backbone [26] on a 10-class PlantVillage tomato subset [4] (9 diseases and healthy; 1,000 training and 100 validation images per class). Pooled 960-d features of the training images and their mirror images (20,000 vectors) train a 960–256–10 MLP head with dropout 0.3, AdamW [27] (learning rate

Validation accuracy is 97.6% (Fig. 9a); because the epoch and the temperature were selected on the same 1,000 images, this figure is optimistic. Lightweight checks flag dark, over-exposed, blurred and leafless photographs.

runs.t: Table III shows that the language layer is the largest single improvement: replacing whole-phrase fuzzy matching with concept-level matching raises description-only accuracy from 63.5% to 92.9%, and the prototype’s matcher remains the bottleneck even when paired with our engine (86.4%). The prototype understood 91.8% of inputs and was confidently wrong on 10.6%; the motivating “white dust” sentence illustrates why: shared filler words gave weight to unrelated ring-spot lay-terms, and a negated clause was ignored entirely (Fig. 3). Dialogue adds 3.9 points, and every configuration built on our matcher is confidently wrong on at most 1.2% of runs. Accuracy is balanced across languages: 96.3% for Tamil, 96.9% for English and 97.4% for Tanglish inputs (prototype: 67.6%, 52.9% and 76.5%). Per disease (Fig. 6), the remaining errors concentrate on bacterial spot (75%) and target spot (89%); the most frequent confusions are bacterial spot
early blight, three diseases that genuinely share small dark, ring-forming lesions with yellow halos in the dataset [17].

runs.t: On a 12-thread laptop CPU without a GPU (Table IV), concept matching takes 2.0 ms, one inference step including the information-gain search 0.84 ms, and a complete diagnosis request through the web API 3.7 ms (median). Photo classification takes 7.1 ms. The system therefore runs on commodity hardware, and the graph can be served from a small server.

The results support the central design choice: a curated, probabilistic KG that reasons over noisy evidence and asks targeted questions is robust where an image classifier alone is brittle, and it explains its answers in the farmer’s language. Several limitations qualify these findings.

items.t: The test descriptions were written by the authors, and the simulated farmer answers according to the KG’s own probabilities; the results therefore measure the reasoning pipeline, not field accuracy. A field study with real farmer descriptions and agronomist-confirmed diagnoses is the necessary next step.

Edge weights are expert estimates seeded from a dataset and extension guidance; Tamil lay-terms cover common usage but not all regional dialects. The learning loop and the curation queue are designed to correct both, but their effect in the field remains to be measured.
The classifier was trained on laboratory images of nine diseases; its validation accuracy is optimistic, and the degradation study approximates, but does not replace, real field photographs.

The Hutton criteria and TOM-CAST were developed for temperate climates and the remaining risk models are heuristics; none has yet been validated against outbreaks in Tamil Nadu. Community outbreak data shown in this paper are simulated.
The Gemini speech front end was not evaluated quantitatively. Dosages are taken from the cited dataset or general guidance and must be checked against product labels and local recommendations.

runs.t: Tomato Doctor combines a probabilistic knowledge graph, concept-level understanding of Tamil, English and Tanglish, Bayesian evidence fusion, cost-aware information-gain questioning, weather-driven priors and spray planning, and confirmation-driven learning. In our evaluation it raises top-1 accuracy from 63.5% to 96.8% over the fuzzy-matching prototype with about two questions, keeps confidently wrong answers near 1%, recovers from degraded photographs through dialogue, and repairs a corrupted graph from farmer feedback. Future work will validate the system with farmers and agronomists in Tamil Nadu, calibrate the risk models against local outbreak records, extend the graph to further crops, and evaluate the speech front end on recorded farmer queries.
